content.thinking:
I need to design a mythic nine-tailed kitsune fox in high-fantasy anime style using toon and glow effects, planning out its proportions—shoulder height around 0.9m, body length 1.4m, with tails fanning up to over 1.6m tall.

Now I'm sketching out the skeleton structure in coordinate space, working through a spine chain built from a catmull-rom path rooted at the hips, deciding how many named joints to assign across the spans to properly reach from hips to chest.

I'm then continuing upward with a neck chain running from chest to head base, two joints spanning the segments, and attaching a head joint off the neck's final point with an appropriate parent reference and direction.

For the head itself, I'm planning a fox-style skull using a scaled sphere, with the muzzle built as a swept loft from the skull front to the nose tip, a separate jaw joint for the lower jaw, a dark nose sphere at the tip, and large triangular kitsune-style ear extrusions.

Now I'm working out ear geometry using extruded outlines with cream/pink inner tufts, tilting them back via the local coordinate axes, and deciding to place them in explicit model-space coordinates attached to the head bone to keep things simple. For the eyes, I'm planning narrow, slanted anime-style eye decals on the skull, sized smaller than typical to fit the fox's features.

For coloring, I'm settling on a kitsune aesthetic: a white-cream coat with soft lavender shading, vermilion-red kumadori markings, gold ornamental accents like bells and tassels, and considering gold-orange or blue-violet spirit flames for the tails.

Now I'm working through the leg structure, using digitigrade hind legs with slender forelimbs, and deciding how to paint the feet—likely dark stockings blended with the cel-shaded coat color via a paint function based on vertical position.

For the front legs, I'm setting the shoulder joint position and planning the limb chain from shoulder to elbow to wrist to paw, trying to get the elbow bending backward naturally like a real fox foreleg while keeping the segment lengths simple.

Checking the geometry further: with lengths 0.34 each, distance 0.65 works with a slight bend, and similarly for the front leg root/target setup distance comes to 0.64, which also allows a believable elbow bend backward. Then I'm placing the paw as a forward-extending capsule near the ground from the wrist position.

I'm settling on coordinate conventions -- using s=1 to mean +X which I'll treat as the left side, naming joints with an "L" suffix accordingly. For the hind legs I'm setting up a three-segment digitigrade chain (hip, knee, hock, foot) with two inner bend directions, positioning the hip and target points and continuing to work out the hock placement.

For skinning, I'm using the limb's output points as a polyline that gets swept with a smoothing radius array to taper the thigh, and I'm setting up the torso as a thick loft along the spine and hip joints to connect the body mass.

Now I'm mapping out the torso path as a catmull curve from rump to chest, swept with an elliptical radius profile and bone-weighted between hips and spine joints -- I need to figure out which joint "owns" the rump region behind the hips since the bone ownership rule assigns overlapping points to whichever joint is listed last at that t-value.

Since the hips joint and spine1 joint share the same t-value, the duplicate-start filter drops the earlier one, so hips gets dropped from the kept spans and spine1 effectively owns that rump region—which is fine since hips ownership there is irrelevant for rigging purposes anyway.

For the nine tails, I'm designing them as separate chains rooted at the hips joint, fanning outward in an arc like a peacock's plumage. Each tail starts near the same base point with slight lateral offsets, curves backward and upward with varying lengths (center tails longest), and the tips rise to roughly 1.75m in height.

Nearly-sideways outer tails work well for a fan-wheel look from the front, but checking the side view, I worry the stack reads flat. I should tilt the fan plane more vertically, more like a peacock's upward sweeping arc, to get better depth from both angles.

Simplifying to discrete points along each tail with pitch and yaw that gradually shift to create a curved, graceful sweep rather than a straight line.

Still working out tail geometry...

I'll need to reduce base radius and widen yaw spacing so the nine tails overlap less while still reading as a fluffy fan, then settle on a naming scheme like tail1_1...tail9_5 for the joint chains, checking they stay unique and valid.

Totaling things up, I land around 75 joints once I count tails, spine, neck, head, jaw, ears, and legs—well within the 160 limit.

For tail coloring, I'm giving a kitsune-style look with cream coats fading into vermilion flame tips near the end of each tail, using a gradient paint sampled at specific points along each tail's path, clamped so it doesn't overshoot past the tip.

I'm also considering adding fur texture detail - scattering small fur tuft cards along each tail sweep, roughly 40 per tail across all nine tails, sharing one material by using a neutral tint since distinct colors would otherwise split into separate draw calls.

Each tuft will be a cream-colored flame-like wisp shape with a shaded lower edge, built as simple flat cards shaded with face normals so lighting reads correctly. Cost-wise this stays cheap since each card is only a handful of triangles, and I'm scattering them across the already-built tail sweep surfaces using the bone frames from the tail chain skin.

For orientation, I want the fur flow to point roughly away from the tail base along each tail's direction rather than a fixed default, since tails fan out in different directions -- so I'm computing flow per-hit as the normalized vector from the tail base to the hit position, which should work reasonably well even for sideways-pointing outer tails.

For the spirit flames at each tail tip, I'm thinking glowing teardrop-shaped cards with a flame texture in teal/violet/white tones, oriented to always face upward since flames rise regardless of tail angle.

I want each flame rigidly attached to its tail's last joint using a bone binding option, with one shared texture and tint across all nine tails so the material and glow effect are reused rather than duplicated. I'm also considering layering teal and whitish flame shapes within the same texture for more visual depth.

I'll alternate two flame color textures—cyan and violet-blue—across the nine tails, then add six small floating hitodama orbs hovering around the fox at varying heights, each parented to a nearby joint and using the same flame-card glow technique at a smaller scale.

I also want to arrange these orbs in a loose helix on the front and sides, keeping the body's bounding radius reasonable, and add a small gold tiara ornament with a glowing gem on the forehead as another accent.

Now I'm planning the kitsune-style markings: red facial stripes under the eyes, a forehead mark, and flame-swirl decals on the torso flanks, applied via SVG decal textures with mirrored placement, plus painted leg bands. I'm also thinking about adding a shimenawa-style rope collar with paper shide for the neck.

Writing collar details... adding gold beaded necklace sweep, tassel/bell pendant, and hanging zigzag shide paper cards along the rope. I'm also planning gold ankle rings on the legs via a loop sweep on the leg joints.

For the tail, I'll add thin gold bands near the base of each tail using a loop cut restricted to that tail's own sweep mesh, anchored at a frame point along the tail chain, then sweeping a thin tube around that loop path.

Now I'm planning face details — eyes, nose, mouth line, whiskers, cheek fur tufts via scattered fur cards, brow markings, and kitsune-style ears with cream fur and black tips reminiscent of Ninetales.

Deciding ears should be cream outside with a vermilion gradient tip and pink-cream inner fur, using a procedural paint function based on extrude position. I'm sizing the fox head stylized and large for anime proportions, working out skull radius, muzzle length, overall body length, and total model dimensions to keep it looking like a big fox.

Now I'm working out the precise joint hierarchy and coordinates: placing the neck, head joint, skull center, and muzzle positions with specific radii so the fox carries its head high and the muzzle tapers naturally toward the nose.

Setting up the section orientation and then sketching the lower jaw as its own sweep attached to the jaw bone, running from the chin joint forward with tapering radii, keeping the mouth closed for the rest pose.

For the mouth itself, I'm thinking a thin dark line along the muzzle underside rather than a full open interior, with a lower lip overlap near the chin. I'm defining the face paint as mostly cream for a white fox coat, picking a base color and letting shadow tones auto-shift toward violet for fur contrast.

Now I'm settling on a countershaded palette: a cream base with a golden-peach tone warming the back and fading toward white on the belly, applied through a fur-edge gradient technique with zigzag teeth for that anime-style fur edge. I'm also picking accent colors for the fox's markings — vermilion, deep crimson, and gold tones for the ear tips and other highlights.

Working out the paint logic for the body coat using the fur-edge zigzag along the vertical axis so the back reads peach and the belly cream, and now thinking through how to adapt that same technique for the tails which are tilted differently from the body.

For the tail coat, I'm nesting gradients so the color transitions from peach to cream near the root, then shifts to vermilion at the tip, verifying the blend resolution handles stacked gradients correctly when the outer paint's inputs are themselves paints.

For cel shading, I'm defining how a lit paint resolves: if the surface normal aligns enough with the light it stays lit, otherwise it falls into shadow using a darker version of the resolved color — this handles the vermilion tips darkening appropriately in shadow.

Now for the head/face region, I'm using a position-based fur edge pattern along the vertical axis to split peach forehead fur from cream muzzle fur, with jagged teeth parameters controlling the edge transition.

For eye placement, I'm positioning decals on the skull sphere using spherical coordinates — mirrored left/right, angled forward with a slight elevation and a slanted roll to give the fox eyes their characteristic tilt, while sizing them small relative to the skull radius.

I'll guess roll applies after the mirror, so for the left eye (s=1) a positive roll rotates CCW with the right side up, putting the outer corner on the viewer's right correctly for that mirrored eye — risky but acceptable. I also need to confirm the decal projects onto the skull surface itself along the default direction, not onto the muzzle or brow.

For eyes, I'm picking amber iris with a pink blush, since teal/violet spirit flames complement vermilion/gold trim better than another warm tone. Eye glow isn't paintable, so I'll skip that detail.

For the ears, I'm defining the kitsune-style triangular ear outline with tufts in the forward-facing plane, using model-left as x and up as y.

Checking placement math for the cross product of the x and y vectors confirms the ear faces forward correctly on the right side (s=1), but on the mirrored left side (s=-1) the orientation flips and ends up facing backward — I need to fix that asymmetry.

Actually, a simpler fix: determine inner vs outer by comparing the normal against a fixed forward direction, so whichever side faces forward gets the inner pink color and the back gets the outer coat color, regardless of mirroring.

Refining the inner/outer paint logic with a deeper vermilion tip color, then wrapping the flat colors through cel-shading based on normals. Now I need to set up the ear joints for the rig, adding hinge joints at the ear base parented to the head bone.

I'm planning cream fur tufts at the ear base using small extruded card geometry, plus gold hoop earrings with a swept circular path and a hanging tassel card attached below each ring.

Now I'm figuring out a forehead ornament placement near the skull's front-top, combining a crescent-moon extrude with a gem circle oriented outward, computing the surface hit point and orientation vectors for the attachment frame.

I'm cross-checking the thickness axis math to confirm it matches the surface normal, then planning a small vermilion teardrop decal for the forehead mark itself.

For the facial decals, I want a flame-shaped vermilion mark with a gold dot on the forehead, plus red kumadori stripes sweeping back from the outer eye corners on the cheeks, mirrored left and right using hit-based positioning on the skull. I'm also considering adding backward-angled card spikes along the lower skull sides as a fur ruff detail.

Now for the body decals: I'm placing flame/swirl vermilion patterns on the torso flanks, mirrored on both sides, plus vermilion paint bands with a gold cuff ring on the forelegs, cream coloring on the belly, and blending thigh sweeps into the hip area.

I'm defining the torso's radius profile along the spine from rump to chest, setting rx/ry values at each key point (rump, hips, mid-body, chest, neck) to shape the body silhouette smoothly.

Now I'm working out the neck taper and adding a fluffy cream ruff around the base using a ring of leaning fur cards attached to the neck bone's tangent frame.

Tapering the neck to 0.085 near the skull, then moving to leg proportions—foreleg radii stepping down from shoulder to wrist along the swept chain. For coloring I'm working out the sock boundary logic, using a position-based cel edge along the vertical axis to split cream above from dark stocking below.

Still writing fur edge logic...

Adding a few scattered fur tufts near the hind leg elbows and chest ruff to break up the silhouette.

Now I'm shaping the paws themselves, defining each foot as a small capsule sweeping from ankle to toe so it sits flush with the ground plane at the contact point.

Still placing toe spheres and claws...

I need to figure out the parent joints for each leg chain: hind legs should parent off the hips joint, while front legs should parent off the chest/spine3 joint since that's closest to the shoulders in z-position. I'm working out how the limb function takes a root, target, and segment lengths to generate the chain points.

I'm also adding small details like thin whisker tubes extending from the muzzle sides, and tiny downward-pointing fang spikes placed just below the muzzle edge for visible teeth.

Checking the jaw placement, I notice the fang spikes and lower jaw overlap with the muzzle underside, which actually works fine since it reads as a closed mouth, but I decide to shift the jaw center lower and adjust its path and radii so the proportions look cleaner.

Checking the geometry, the mouth seam line falls outside the muzzle ellipse's radius so it would be hidden—I'll drop that idea and instead drape an upper-lip path onto the muzzle surface, sweeping ink along it so it conforms to the nearest surface points.

For the nose, I'm making a small dark sphere flattened slightly, colored deep plum, and considering a tiny highlight but may skip it since the brow markings are already handled by the eye texture.

Now I'm planning gold tail accessories—rings with small hanging tassels or beads on each tail.

For the tail ring design, I'll add a secondary thin red ring slightly offset from the gold one for color banding. For flame effects, I'm placing flame cards at the tail tips plus smaller flickering wisps scattered along the last quarter of each tail for a glowing wreath effect.

Writing flame SVG paths...

I'm defining color variants for the flame layers — teal and violet versions each with outer, mid, and core hues for a hard-edged anime fire look, no outlines. For the cards, I'll use a crossed billboard setup facing up so the flame reads from all angles, sized for the tail tip placement with a small sink offset.

Smaller floating orb flames could work as hitodama effects, and I'm confirming the glow function accepts arrays of card meshes fine. For tail fur, I'm leaning toward greyscale tuft textures that get tinted by a color string or Paint reference at the card root, so the fur color can be customized without redrawing the texture.

Using a non-cel gradient paint for tuft cards so they match the tail coat's gradient, even though the tail body itself is cel-shaded with flat baked colors — the slight lighting mismatch between flat cel shading and standard material should be acceptable visually. Now I'm sketching out the SVG path for the tuft shape itself, a leaf-like fur wisp.

I'm sanity-checking part and triangle budgets: estimating roughly 250 parts total across torso, decals, legs, and card-based tufts/flames, which should stay well under the 1000-part limit.

Still tallying triangle counts... planning to scatter around 36 fur cards along each tail sweep, and considering whether to add extra decal stripes on the torso.

For the neck, I'm building a twisted rope collar using a closed sweep loop around the neck, painting alternating vermilion and cream stripes along its length to mimic a twisted-cord pattern, accepting a minor seam artifact where the stripes wrap.

For the hanging bell, I'm figuring out where on the neck tube to anchor it at the lowest front point, working out the azimuth and elevation needed since the neck leans forward and the tube's clock orientation determines which side faces front versus back.

I'll place the bell using the point's own moved offset so it sits properly along the neck's outward normal, then add the bell geometry, slit, and small ring before working on the hanging shide tassels attached near the rope points, using frames oriented downward for a natural lean.

For the rope knots, I'll generate nine points along the path and convert each into a frame that inherits the path's local orientation, then select just the front five for hanging the shide. Now I'm sketching out the zigzag paper strip texture for the shide using a small SVG template.

Writing zigzag SVG path...

Designing a simple tassel ornament with a gold knob and cap at top plus fanning red strands below, sized for the 128px raster. I'm considering placing these tassels at the bell bottom, earring bottom, and possibly hanging from the tail rings for a natural decorative touch.

I'm now reconsidering the tail placement and thinking instead about adding flowing ribbon streamers from the collar, sweeping back along the flanks as a flattened membrane shape between curved path edges, keeping them clear of the torso's silhouette so they float naturally alongside the body.

I'll add three sash loops - a thicker red center band with thin gold trim at top and bottom - plus a decorative bow at the back made of two vermilion sphere knots with ribbon tails extruding down behind the tail base, placed near the top of the torso.

Still building the ribbon geometry... now I'm shifting to actually writing the code, being careful with the chain/joint API calls for the neck segments and head joint attachment, keeping strict TypeScript happy by avoiding unused names.

Setting up more joints for jaw and ears, then starting the tail chain attached to hips...

I'm working out tail base positions and writing a path function that computes curvature using angle offsets per segment index, tapering outward from the center.

Still writing tail math...

I'm checking that the outer tails don't collide with the hind leg/hip geometry, tracking their lateral and height positions as u increases, and confirming the clearance looks fine before moving on to the drawing order of the tails.

The center tail (k=0) points straight back and up, curving from 58° to 82°. I'm setting up the radius profile for a smooth tapering tube with a pointed tip cap, and planning to keep the side detail at 8 segments while thinking about how to apply gradient coloring along each tail's path.

For the painting, I'll build a Catmull-Rom path for each tail and sweep a tube mesh along it, sampling colors from the gradient at each point. I'm also considering adding thin vermilion ring markings near the tip of each tail by checking the parametric position along the sweep and overlaying stripe bands at specific t-ranges.

Adjusting the fur-edge threshold so peach stays mostly on the top with cream dominating the sides, tuning the level and teeth parameters so the flank transition sits around n.y between -0.2 and 0.1. The body gets a similar fur-edge treatment for the neck, but I don't need it on the head.

Now I'm planning the helper setup inside build(): defining a seeded RNG and palette locally so results stay deterministic, and figuring out exactly which imports (rng, paint, gradient, catmull, polyline, limb, furEdge, cel, animeEye, glow, INK) I'll actually need versus which to drop to avoid unused-import errors. Writing the import statements and setup code...

Still writing flame SVG path...

Writing decal marking SVGs...

Now I'm sketching out the tail tip fur tuft and eye details, then setting up the torso rig with a hip joint and spine chain built from a catmull-rom curve through several points, checking whether the chain's optional group parameter is worth using or better left out to limit risk.

Defining torso sweep and radius profile...

Still tuning radii profile...

Now I'm sweeping the neck tube with tapering radii and thinking through the cap style so it joins cleanly into the torso's chest end without leaving a visible seam.

I'm placing the skull sphere part on the head bone with scale values that shape it, confirming the joint position makes sense anatomically. For cheek ruff I'm scattering fluff cards filtered to skull hit points near the sides and below a certain height.

I'm setting the fluff flow direction, size, lean, bend and density for the tufts with a cream tint. The eyes, brows and muzzle colors I'm handling with cel shading and fur-edge blending between peach and cream tones for the nose bridge.

Now I'm writing the leg-building loop that mirrors limb placement for left and right sides using position and size parameters.

I'm working through the bend-direction format for limb joints, deciding whether to pass a single direction or a list of directions for the elbow and knee bends, then figuring out how the chain function will consume the resulting point array for each leg segment.

I'm setting up the sweep radii for the foreleg so the shoulder joint tapers smoothly into the torso surface, checking that the top radius stays small enough relative to the torso's radius so the leg appears to emerge naturally from the chest rather than poking through it.

Now I'm building the paw as a capsule from wrist to toe, giving it a dark plum sock colour for contrast against the leg, then adding three toe spheres and forward-pointing claw spikes to finish the foot detail.

Still writing bangle rings...

For the hind legs, I'm applying similar bangles at the cannon bone height and scattering fur tufts on the back of the thigh using a filtered surface scatter, leaning them toward a downward-back flow direction, then defining the taper radii for the hind leg sweep.

I'm placing the hip joints at x ±0.14, matching the torso's haunch radius, and working out the digitigrade foot structure: the metatarsal runs vertically down to the foot joint, then the paw capsule extends forward from there to form the toes. I'm verifying the hind chain naming (hip/knee/hock/foot) spans correctly to four points with proper parenting.

Now I'm designing a gold tiara ornament for the forehead — generating a crescent moon shape by plotting outer and inner arc points at offset radii and angles to create the curved horn silhouette.

Then I'm adding a small glowing teal gem embedded at the center of the forehead decoration, alongside the crescent and decal mark.

I'm placing the crescent on the skull surface using a sampled hit point, then computing a tangent "up" vector from the surface normal to orient the extrusion correctly along the head's curvature.

For the cheek decals, I'm using the hit position and normal with mirroring for left/right symmetry, and thinking through how the line direction in the original SVG path should map onto the face depending on which side it's viewed from.

I'm checking the eye placement against the muzzle geometry, computing coordinates to make sure the eyes sit correctly at the front-sides of the skull without overlapping the muzzle's starting radius.

Widening the eye azimuth slightly to around 40° to avoid clipping. I'm also setting up the forehead flame mark decal position and size, then moving on to work out the tail flame placement at the tip of the bone chain.

Adding wisp effects now...

Now placing hitodama orbs floating around the front of the body, alternating colors and sizes, anchored to the spine joint, while checking that their positions keep everything above the floor and within the overall silhouette width.

For the tails, I'm adding small perpendicular rings looped around each tail at specific points along its curve, using golden and vermilion bands with thin radii, weighted smoothly against the nearby bone joints.

Now I'm working on the torso sash — a loop around the body at the spine2 joint, cutting a perpendicular cross-section that stays confined to the torso surface. I need to figure out the sweep's cross-section orientation since the binormal direction around a closed loop like this isn't fixed relative to the body.

For the band itself I'll use a circle section of radius 0.022 colored vermillion, flanked by two thinner gold loops offset slightly forward and back along the body, radius 0.01. Now I'm thinking through how to place a bow or knot on the back, using a ray cast downward from above the body to find where it intersects the skin surface.

Then I need to set up loops and a small gold sphere for the knot center, positioning the bow loops symmetrically to either side of that hit point using offsets and scale, with slight rotations to splay them outward, and extending ribbon tail curves downward from the knot using a smooth spline through a few points below it.

Checking the ribbon tail geometry against the torso's curved surface, I realize the tail path at x=0.10 dips inside the torso surface rather than following its exterior, so I'm adjusting the x-offset outward to about 0.12 to keep the ribbon properly draped on the outside of the torso curve.

Skipping the pendant for now, keeping gold trim on the sash, and adding whiskers as rods from the muzzle. For fur, I'm scattering chest ruff cards near the front torso using a filter based on height and normal direction, with angled leaning and specific flow direction, around 25 cards, and considering belly feathering next.

Tail fur comes to about 270 cards total. I'm also adding leg fur and fox-ear tufts, while letting the flank swirl decal handle any dorsal striping. For the shoulder area, I'm placing a smaller vermilion swirl decal near the foreleg's upper sweep, checking that the target point sits close enough to the leg surface given its taper from root to tip.

Given the risk of the decal projection failing to find surface hits on such a small patch, I'm deciding to skip the shoulder decals entirely and instead add vermilion paint bands directly on the legs alongside the existing sock and gold bangle markings. I'm defining the fur card helper inline rather than as a separate function, skipping ear tuft placement at the base, and writing an SVG tuft texture shaped like a feathery blade with a soft stroke down the center, tinted per card.

Now I'm working out how to build the gold earrings: writing a helper that generates a circular ring path from a center point and two perpendicular direction vectors, then feeding those points into a closed Catmull-Rom spline. I'm positioning the earring hoop just outside the ear's base, calculating the offset coordinates and orienting the ring's plane to face laterally outward from the head.

Still defining ear geometry...

Checking the ear tilt axes now—mirroring the x-direction for symmetry and confirming the outward y-tilt makes sense for both sides.

For the ear coloring, I realize there's a sign bug: the front-facing normal flips with the mirror parameter s, so my fixed inner-color test (n.z > threshold) will land on the wrong face for the right ear. I need to make the test depend on s itself so it correctly picks the front side regardless of mirroring.

Writing the ear paint function...

Adding more swirl decals...

Working out the frame type signatures for b.along, verifying that the callback gives a point I can use to build frames for the rope knots, pushing each into an array manually since the return type isn't guaranteed to collect them.

For placement, I'm filtering which frames sit on the front/visible side of the neck loop by comparing z-coordinates against the loop's center, so the shide only appear facing outward rather than hidden behind the mane. Next I'm setting up the neck surface from the neck tube to build that loop.

Writing rope sweep code...

Then I want to scatter gold beads along the rope path, spacing out a set number of small sphere parts bound to points along the sweep so they follow the rope's frame.

Now I'm working out the bell placement — positioning it on the underside of the neck tube using the clock angle convention, then offsetting the bell center downward with a slit cutout and a ring above, plus a tassel hanging from the bell's bottom frame.

Writing tail chain loop code...

Still computing tail point positions...

I'm checking the geometry: center tail goes straight back with yaw angle zero while outer tails fan outward, and elevation sweeps from about 58° to 82°, giving a tip height around 1.8m for the center and roughly 2.1m total once the flame extends above it.

Trimming the center tail length a bit brings the full model to a more sensible 2.0m with orbs reaching up to 1.4m. I'm working out scaling factors for tail tube radii across segments, shrinking flame sizes per tail index, and setting tuft scales, then defining how scattered cards sit on the tail's surface with tinted paint pulled from the root gradient.

Now I'm setting the random seed for scatter distribution and minimum spacing, then moving into the hind thigh and chest fur cards with a warm cream tint. I'm checking the limb import path, then building the neck ruff using ring geometry—placing two rings at different positions along the neck with alternating radii, feeding their items into the card system with specific size, lean, bend, and spin settings so the fur flows naturally outward and flattens against the surface, plus sizing up the chest ruff a bit lower on the body before starting on the whisker generation loop.

Writing whisker rod code...

Then I'm considering whether to add a glowing magic circle of runes on the floor beneath the fox for a summoned-spirit effect, but deciding to keep things simple and skip the extra floor decal for now, focusing instead on making sure the fox has proper floor contact.

Shifting to the hitodama spirit orbs, I'm planning teal and violet flame textures attached to a spine joint, with elevated glow strength, plus a small gold magatama necklace detail while skipping a crown. Now I'm computing the outline points for a crescent shape, stepping through angles from 195 to 345 degrees to build the outer curve coordinates.

Checking that the inner arc points reverse correctly and close properly against the outer arc to form a valid 18-point crescent opening upward. I'm placing this extruded crescent near the head bone using a frame offset and tangent orientation, with gold coloring and thin bevel settings, confirming the hit point's normal vector works for positioning and that the point input type accepts frame-based positions.

I'm deciding on shading strategy: using cel shading for large flat-colored surfaces like gold sweeps and torso, but keeping small parts like claws and paws as flat single colors to manage texel density and stay within the color budget, before finalizing the material assignments.

Setting up imports for geometry, builder, IK limbs, math helpers, paint/texture tools, and toon shading kit...

Defining the color palette with cream, peach, vermillion, gold, pink, teal, violet and bone tones...

Still defining fur paints...

Simplifying to a straightforward gradient so the hind legs shade smoothly from peach at the top to cream lower down.

Now I'm setting the neck color to match the coat and the jaw to cream, then building the torso sweep along a curved spine path with a coat-colored fill and radius function controlling its taper.

For the skull and surface features, I'm placing the cheek decal using a spherical coordinate hit on the skin surface, making sure the decal target and size parameters line up with the surface API, and adjusting the eye roll offset slightly with the side multiplier.

Now I'm structuring the full build function — setting up the builder, palette, textures, and skeleton joints with the hip position, then defining the neck chain using a smooth curved path through several points.

Still writing skeleton joints...

Writing collar paint logic now, then sash ribbons by raycasting the torso surface to find attachment points and draping a catmull-rom path downward with slight outward lift for each side.

For the bow loops, I'm placing scaled sphere geometries near the top of the ribbons and rotating them about the Z axis so each loop tilts outward and upward symmetrically for left and right sides.

Confirming the knot sits as a gold sphere, bones attach to the spine joints, and I'm continuing to define remaining elements like orb positions and ear joints for the head.

For the muzzle sweep, I'm checking that the radius function's return type correctly matches the expected tuple shape through contextual typing, since TypeScript should infer the tuple from the function signature rather than defaulting to a plain array.

I'm now sweeping the jaw geometry with its own path and tapering radius, attached to the jaw bone and tinted cream, while skipping tongue, lower teeth, and chin fur details for now. Then I move into drawing the tassel SVG...

Now I'm roughing out the overall part count for the full file—torso, decals, neck, ruff cards, head elements, ears, and the tails each with their own tube, cards, flame, and ring components—to make sure the structure stays organized before writing it all out.

Still working through the geometry helpers... I'm checking the types and parameters flowing into the card and wisp positioning functions, making sure offsets along normals and tangent directions at specific points on the tail chain produce the right placement for the wispy elements trailing off the tails.
